title: Task: Implement benchmark runner CLI with warmup and reporting
description:
## Task: Implement Benchmark Runner

Create CLI harness that runs benchmarks consistently across all model types,
using the unified Embedder trait from bd-2crr.

## CLI Interface
```bash
xf benchmark --model=all-MiniLM-L6-v2 --corpus=tests/fixtures/benchmark_corpus.json
xf benchmark --model=static-retrieval-mrl-en-v1 --dimensions=256
xf benchmark --compare --models=miniLM,bge-small,static-mrl --output=results.json
xf benchmark --reranker=flashrank --query="test query" --corpus=tests/fixtures/benchmark_corpus.json
```

## Output Type: BenchmarkResult

This is the primary output struct consumed by bd-5fj3 (report generator).
It aggregates all per-run metrics into a single serializable record per model.

```rust
use crate::models::ModelCategory;
use crate::benchmark::metrics::{SpeedMetrics, QualityMetrics};

/// Complete benchmark result for one model, consumed by report generator (bd-5fj3)
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct BenchmarkResult {
    pub model_name: String,
    pub category: ModelCategory,  // From bd-2crr: StaticEmbedder or TransformerEmbedder
    pub eligible: bool,           // release_date >= 2025-11-01 (from candidates list)
    pub release_date: Option<String>,

    // Quality metrics (from corpus evaluation)
    pub quality: QualityMetrics,

    // Speed metrics (from benchmark phases)
    pub speed: SpeedMetrics,

    // Reliability metrics
    pub total_requests: usize,
    pub errors: usize,
    pub oom_count: usize,
    pub panics: usize,

    // Resource usage
    pub peak_rss_mb: f64,
    pub steady_rss_mb: f64,
    pub model_file_size_mb: f64,
    pub peak_threads: usize,

    // MRL analysis (if model supports_mrl)
    pub mrl_dims_tested: Vec<usize>,
    pub mrl_quality_at_dims: Vec<(usize, f64)>,  // (dims, ndcg@10)

    // Reranker-specific (only for reranker benchmarks)
    pub reranker_lift: Option<f64>,  // % lift in NDCG@10 vs no-rerank
}

impl BenchmarkResult {
    /// Error rate as fraction (0.0-1.0)
    pub fn error_rate(&self) -> f64 {
        if self.total_requests == 0 { return 0.0; }
        self.errors as f64 / self.total_requests as f64
    }

    /// Is this result reliable enough for winner selection?
    pub fn is_reliable(&self) -> bool {
        self.error_rate() < 0.01 && self.oom_count == 0 && self.panics == 0
    }
}
```

## Implementation
Uses the Embedder and Reranker traits from bd-2crr (ModelRegistry) to load models.
No redundant trait - the benchmark runner is a consumer of the trait interfaces.

```rust
use crate::models::{Embedder, Reranker, ModelRegistry, ModelCategory};

struct BenchmarkRun {
    model: Box<dyn Embedder>,
    corpus: Corpus,
    config: BenchmarkConfig,
    collector: MetricCollector, // from bd-164
}

impl BenchmarkRun {
    /// Execute full benchmark and produce BenchmarkResult
    pub fn execute(&mut self) -> Result<BenchmarkResult> {
        // 1. Cold start phase
        let cold_start = self.measure_cold_start()?;

        // 2. Warmup phase (discard metrics)
        for _ in 0..self.config.warmup_iterations {
            self.model.embed_batch(&self.corpus.sample_batch())?;
        }

        // 3. Measurement phase
        let mut latencies = Vec::with_capacity(self.config.measure_iterations);
        let mut errors = 0usize;
        let mut oom_count = 0usize;

        for _ in 0..self.config.measure_iterations {
            let batch = self.corpus.sample_batch();
            let start = Instant::now();
            match self.model.embed_batch(&batch) {
                Ok(_) => latencies.push(start.elapsed()),
                Err(e) if is_oom(&e) => { oom_count += 1; errors += 1; }
                Err(_) => { errors += 1; }
            }
        }

        // 4. Quality evaluation (using ground truth from corpus)
        let quality = self.evaluate_quality()?;

        // 5. MRL sweep (if supported)
        let (mrl_dims, mrl_quality) = if self.model.supports_mrl() {
            self.mrl_sweep(&[64, 128, 256, 512, 768, 1024])?
        } else {
            (vec![], vec![])
        };

        // 6. Resource measurement
        let rss = get_process_rss_mb();

        Ok(BenchmarkResult {
            model_name: self.model.model_name().to_string(),
            category: self.model.category(),  // From Embedder trait
            eligible: self.config.candidates.is_eligible(&self.model.model_name()),
            release_date: self.config.candidates.release_date(&self.model.model_name()),
            quality,
            speed: SpeedMetrics {
                cold_start_ms: cold_start.as_secs_f64() * 1000.0,
                warm_latency_p50_ms: percentile(&latencies, 0.50),
                warm_latency_p95_ms: percentile(&latencies, 0.95),
                warm_latency_p99_ms: percentile(&latencies, 0.99),
                throughput_docs_per_sec: compute_throughput(&latencies, self.config.batch_size),
                time_to_first_result_ms: cold_start.as_secs_f64() * 1000.0 + latencies[0].as_secs_f64() * 1000.0,
            },
            total_requests: self.config.measure_iterations,
            errors,
            oom_count,
            panics: 0,
            peak_rss_mb: rss,
            steady_rss_mb: rss * 0.9,  // Approximation
            model_file_size_mb: self.model_file_size_mb(),
            peak_threads: rayon::current_num_threads(),
            mrl_dims_tested: mrl_dims,
            mrl_quality_at_dims: mrl_quality,
            reranker_lift: None,
        })
    }
}
```

### Benchmark phases
1. Cold start: model load + first embed (measures TTFR)
2. Warmup: 10 iterations (discard, allows JIT/cache warmup)
3. Measurement: 100 iterations with percentile tracking
4. Quality evaluation: using ground truth corpus from bd-cy0
5. MRL sweep: if model supports_mrl(), benchmark at multiple dims
6. Optional rerank phase: if --reranker specified
7. Report generation: JSON + Markdown + terminal summary

### Warmup Strategy
- Separate cold vs warm timings (critical for static vs transformer comparison)
- Capture TTFR (Time to First Result) as distinct metric
- Record CPU/core count and thread pool size
- Log whether ONNX runtime uses AVX2/AVX-512

## Output Formats
- JSON: machine-readable `Vec<BenchmarkResult>` with full metric breakdown
- Markdown: human-readable comparison table
- Terminal: colored summary with winner highlights
- JSONL trace: raw per-iteration latencies for offline analysis

### JSON Output Schema (consumed by bd-5fj3 report)
```json
{
  "timestamp": "2026-01-23T...",
  "system": { "cpu_model": "...", "cores": 8, "ram_gb": 32 },
  "results": [
    {
      "model_name": "static-retrieval-mrl-en-v1",
      "category": "StaticEmbedder",
      "eligible": true,
      "release_date": "2025-11-15",
      "quality": { "ndcg_at_10": 0.72, "mrr_at_10": 0.68, ... },
      "speed": { "warm_latency_p50_ms": 2.1, ... },
      "total_requests": 100,
      "errors": 0,
      "oom_count": 0,
      "peak_rss_mb": 45.2,
      "mrl_dims_tested": [64, 128, 256, 512, 768],
      "mrl_quality_at_dims": [[256, 0.69], [512, 0.71]],
      ...
    }
  ]
}
```

## Location
src/benchmark/runner.rs + src/benchmark/reporter.rs

## Validation and Tests
### Unit tests
- Warmup iterations not included in measurement statistics
- Metric percentile calculations correct (use known distributions)
- BenchmarkResult.error_rate() computation correct
- BenchmarkResult.is_reliable() thresholds correct
- category() populated from Embedder trait
- eligible flag set from candidates list
- Output JSON schema matches expected structure
- Reporter generates valid Markdown tables
- MRL dimension sweep produces correct number of measurements
- TTFR captured separately from steady-state

### Integration tests
- Tiny dataset (10 texts) run completes successfully
- JSON and Markdown reporters produce non-empty valid output
- --compare mode generates comparison table
- Reranker benchmark captures pair scoring metrics
- BenchmarkResult round-trips through serde_json

### E2E script (detailed logging)
```bash
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail
LOG="tests/e2e/results/benchmark_runner_$(date +%Y%m%d_%H%M%S).log"
log() { echo "[$(date +%H:%M:%S)] $*" | tee -a "$LOG"; }
PASS=0; FAIL=0

log "=== Benchmark Runner E2E ==="

# ENV logging
log "System: $(uname -m), $(nproc) cores, $(free -g | awk '/Mem:/{print $2}')GB RAM"
log "ONNX features: $(cat /proc/cpuinfo | grep -o 'avx2\|avx512' | sort -u | tr '\n' ' ')"

# Model discovery
log "Available models:"
xf models list --json 2>/dev/null | jq -r '.[] | "  \(.name) [\(.category)]"' | tee -a "$LOG"

# Single model benchmark
log "Running single-model benchmark..."
xf benchmark --model=all-MiniLM-L6-v2 \
    --corpus=tests/fixtures/benchmark_corpus.json \
    --output=/tmp/bench_single.json 2>&1 | tee -a "$LOG"
[ -f /tmp/bench_single.json ] && { log "  Output file created"; ((PASS++)); } || { log "  No output"; ((FAIL++)); }

# Verify BenchmarkResult schema
log "Validating result schema..."
jq -e '.results[0].model_name' /tmp/bench_single.json >/dev/null && { log "  model_name present"; ((PASS++)); } || ((FAIL++))
jq -e '.results[0].category' /tmp/bench_single.json >/dev/null && { log "  category present"; ((PASS++)); } || ((FAIL++))
jq -e '.results[0].speed.warm_latency_p50_ms' /tmp/bench_single.json >/dev/null && { log "  speed metrics present"; ((PASS++)); } || ((FAIL++))
jq -e '.results[0].quality.ndcg_at_10' /tmp/bench_single.json >/dev/null && { log "  quality metrics present"; ((PASS++)); } || ((FAIL++))

# Comparison mode
log "Running comparison benchmark..."
xf benchmark --compare --models=miniLM,static-mrl \
    --corpus=tests/fixtures/benchmark_corpus.json \
    --output=/tmp/bench_compare.json 2>&1 | tee -a "$LOG"
NRESULTS=$(jq '.results | length' /tmp/bench_compare.json 2>/dev/null)
[ "$NRESULTS" -ge 2 ] && { log "  Comparison has $NRESULTS results"; ((PASS++)); } || { log "  Too few results: $NRESULTS"; ((FAIL++)); }

# MRL sweep
log "Running MRL sweep..."
xf benchmark --model=static-retrieval-mrl-en-v1 --dimensions=256,512,768 \
    --corpus=tests/fixtures/benchmark_corpus.json \
    --output=/tmp/bench_mrl.json 2>&1 | tee -a "$LOG"
MRL_DIMS=$(jq '.results[0].mrl_dims_tested | length' /tmp/bench_mrl.json 2>/dev/null)
[ "$MRL_DIMS" -ge 3 ] && { log "  MRL sweep: $MRL_DIMS dimensions tested"; ((PASS++)); } || { log "  MRL sweep incomplete"; ((FAIL++)); }

# Reranker benchmark
log "Running reranker benchmark..."
xf benchmark --reranker=flashrank \
    --corpus=tests/fixtures/benchmark_corpus.json \
    --output=/tmp/bench_rerank.json 2>&1 | tee -a "$LOG"

# Reliability: error_rate and is_reliable
log "Checking reliability fields..."
ERROR_RATE=$(jq '.results[0].errors / .results[0].total_requests' /tmp/bench_single.json 2>/dev/null)
log "  Error rate: $ERROR_RATE"

log "========================="
log "Results: $PASS passed, $FAIL failed"
exit $FAIL
```

title: Add rich_rust dependency and feature flags
description:
## Objective
Add the `rich_rust` crate as an optional dependency with proper feature flags for conditional compilation.

## Changes to Cargo.toml
```toml
[dependencies]
# Terminal output (keep existing for fallback)
colored = "2.1"
indicatif = "0.17"
console = "0.15"

# Rich terminal output (optional)
rich_rust = { version = "0.1", optional = true, features = ["full"] }

# Terminal detection (used by output module)
terminal_size = "0.4"

# Lazy initialization for compiled regexes
once_cell = "1.19"

[features]
default = []

# Enable rich_rust styled output
rich = ["dep:rich_rust"]

# Full feature set
full = ["rich"]

# Legacy colored output (uses colored crate, no rich_rust)
legacy-colors = []
```

## Conditional Compilation
```rust
// In src/output/mod.rs
#[cfg(feature = "rich")]
use rich_rust::prelude::*;

#[cfg(not(feature = "rich"))]
mod fallback {
    // Minimal fallback implementations when rich_rust is not enabled
}

// Feature detection at runtime
pub fn is_rich_available() -> bool {
    cfg!(feature = "rich")
}
```

## Build Configurations
1. **Default** (`cargo build`): Uses colored crate, no rich_rust
2. **Rich** (`cargo build --features rich`): Uses rich_rust for styled output
3. **Full** (`cargo build --features full`): All features enabled
4. **Legacy** (`cargo build --features legacy-colors`): Uses colored crate explicitly

## Testing
### Build Tests
```bash
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail
LOG=/tmp/xf-deps-test.log
echo "[$(date -Iseconds)] Testing dependency configurations" | tee $LOG

# Test 1: Default build (no features)
echo "Test 1: Default build" | tee -a $LOG
cargo build 2>&1 | tail -5 | tee -a $LOG
if [ $? -eq 0 ]; then echo "  PASS: Default build succeeds" | tee -a $LOG; fi

# Test 2: Rich feature build
echo "Test 2: Rich feature build" | tee -a $LOG
cargo build --features rich 2>&1 | tail -5 | tee -a $LOG
if [ $? -eq 0 ]; then echo "  PASS: Rich feature build succeeds" | tee -a $LOG; fi

# Test 3: Full feature build
echo "Test 3: Full feature build" | tee -a $LOG
cargo build --features full 2>&1 | tail -5 | tee -a $LOG
if [ $? -eq 0 ]; then echo "  PASS: Full feature build succeeds" | tee -a $LOG; fi

# Test 4: Verify rich_rust is optional
echo "Test 4: Verify rich_rust is optional" | tee -a $LOG
cargo tree -p xf --features "" 2>&1 | grep -c "rich_rust" || true
cargo tree -p xf --features rich 2>&1 | grep -c "rich_rust" || true
echo "  PASS: Feature gating works" | tee -a $LOG

echo "[$(date -Iseconds)] All dependency tests passed" | tee -a $LOG
```

### Unit Tests
```rust
#[test]
fn test_is_rich_available_returns_correct_value() {
    let available = is_rich_available();
    
    #[cfg(feature = "rich")]
    assert!(available, "Should be true when rich feature is enabled");
    
    #[cfg(not(feature = "rich"))]
    assert!(!available, "Should be false when rich feature is disabled");
}

#[test]
fn test_build_without_rich_feature() {
    // Smoke test that basic Output works without rich_rust
    #[cfg(not(feature = "rich"))]
    {
        let output = Output::new(OutputFormat::Text);
        output.print("Test message");
    }
}
```

## Revision Notes (v2)
- Added `terminal_size` crate for reliable terminal dimension detection
- Added `once_cell` dependency (already in Cargo.toml) for lazy regex compilation
- Clarified that colored/indicatif/console are kept for fallback compatibility
- Added runtime feature detection function `is_rich_available()`

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] rich_rust is optional dependency with "rich" feature
- [ ] terminal_size crate added for dimension detection
- [ ] once_cell used for lazy regex compilation
- [ ] Default build works without rich_rust
- [ ] Rich feature build includes rich_rust
- [ ] Feature detection function works at runtime
- [ ] All build configurations compile successfully
- [ ] Unit tests pass with and without rich feature

## Task: Daemon Service Integration (systemd/launchd)

Provide optional service definitions so users can keep the model daemon warm across sessions, with proper health checks, logging, restart policies, and environment configuration.

```ini
[Unit]
Description=xf Warm Model Daemon
Documentation=man:xf(1)
After=network.target
StartLimitIntervalSec=300
StartLimitBurst=5

[Service]
Type=notify
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/xf daemon start --foreground --systemd
ExecStop=/usr/local/bin/xf daemon stop
ExecReload=/bin/kill -HUP $MAINPID

# Resource management
Nice=10
IOSchedulingClass=idle
IOSchedulingPriority=7
MemoryMax=2G
MemoryHigh=1536M
CPUQuota=200%

# Security hardening
NoNewPrivileges=true
ProtectSystem=strict
ProtectHome=read-only
PrivateTmp=true
ReadWritePaths=/tmp/xf-daemon.sock
ReadWritePaths=%h/.cache/xf

RestartSec=5
WatchdogSec=60

Environment=XF_MODEL_CACHE=%h/.cache/xf/models
```

```rust
// src/daemon/main.rs
pub fn run_daemon(opts: DaemonOpts) -> Result<()> {
    let config = load_daemon_config()?;

    if opts.foreground {
        // Run in foreground (for service managers)
        tracing::info!("Starting xf-daemon in foreground mode");

        if opts.systemd {
            // Notify systemd we are ready
            sd_notify::notify(true, &[sd_notify::NotifyState::Ready])?;

            // Set up watchdog timer
            if let Some(usec) = sd_notify::watchdog_enabled(false) {
                let interval = Duration::from_micros(usec / 2);
                tokio::spawn(async move {
                    loop {
                        sd_notify::notify(false, &[sd_notify::NotifyState::Watchdog]).ok();
                        tokio::time::sleep(interval).await;
                    }
                });
            }
        }

        run_server(config).await?;
    } else {
        // Daemonize (double-fork)
        daemonize(config)?;
    }

    Ok(())
}
```

```rust
// src/daemon/health.rs
pub async fn health_check(socket_path: &Path) -> Result<HealthStatus> {
    let client = DaemonClient::new_with_path(socket_path);
    let timeout = Duration::from_secs(5);

    match tokio::time::timeout(timeout, client.health()).await {
        Ok(Ok(status)) => {
            tracing::info!(
                uptime_secs = status.uptime_secs,
                models_loaded = status.models_loaded,
                memory_mb = status.rss_mb,
                "Daemon healthy"
            );
            Ok(status)
        }
        Ok(Err(e)) => {
            tracing::error!(error = %e, "Daemon unhealthy");
            Err(e)
        }
        Err(_) => {
            tracing::error!("Daemon health check timed out");
            Err(anyhow::anyhow!("Health check timed out after {}s", timeout.as_secs()))
        }
    }
}
```

description:
## Task: Implement mxbai-rerank-xsmall-v1 Backend

Integrate Mixedbread AI ultra-small reranker as an alternative to FlashRank.

## Model Details
- Source: mixedbread-ai/mxbai-rerank-xsmall-v1
- Parameters: ~100M (0.1B)
- Architecture: Cross-encoder optimized for speed
- Speed: ~15ms per query-doc pair on CPU
- Format: ONNX available via optimum export
- License: Apache-2.0
- Max sequence length: 512 tokens

## Why This Model
mxbai-rerank-xsmall sits between FlashRank nano (speed) and full cross-encoders (quality):
- 3x slower than FlashRank nano but significantly better quality
- Top-20 reranking: ~300ms (acceptable for CLI with daemon)
- ONNX-native, no Python dependency
- Same vendor as mxbai embedding models (potential synergy)

## Architecture
```rust
pub struct MxbaiReranker {
    session: ort::Session,
    tokenizer: tokenizers::Tokenizer,
    max_length: usize,       // 512 tokens
    batch_size: usize,       // 16 (smaller batches due to larger model)
    name: String,
}

impl Reranker for MxbaiReranker {
    fn rerank(&self, query: &str, documents: &[&str]) -> Result<Vec<f32>> {
        let mut all_scores = Vec::with_capacity(documents.len());
        
        for chunk in documents.chunks(self.batch_size) {
            // mxbai uses standard cross-encoder format:
            // [CLS] query_tokens [SEP] doc_tokens [SEP]
            let encodings: Vec<_> = chunk.iter()
                .map(|doc| self.tokenizer.encode((query, *doc), true)
                    .map(|e| e.truncate(self.max_length, 0)))
                .collect::<Result<Vec<_>>>()?;
            
            let max_len = encodings.iter().map(|e| e.len()).max().unwrap_or(0);
            
            // Build padded tensors
            let input_ids = build_padded_i64_tensor(&encodings, max_len);
            let attention_mask = build_attention_mask_i64(&encodings, max_len);
            
            // Run ONNX inference
            let outputs = self.session.run(ort::inputs![
                "input_ids" => input_ids,
                "attention_mask" => attention_mask,
            ]?)?;
            
            // mxbai-rerank outputs logits, apply sigmoid for [0,1] scores
            let logits = outputs[0].extract_tensor::<f32>()?;
            for i in 0..chunk.len() {
                all_scores.push(sigmoid(logits[[i, 0]]));
            }
        }
        
        Ok(all_scores)
    }
    
    fn model_name(&self) -> &str { &self.name }
    fn max_length(&self) -> usize { self.max_length }
}
```

## Comparison Matrix
| Model | Params | Per-Pair | Top-20 Total | Quality |
|-------|--------|----------|--------------|---------|
| FlashRank nano | ~4M | 5ms | ~100ms | Baseline |
| mxbai-xsmall | 100M | 15ms | ~300ms | +10-15% |
| ms-marco-MiniLM-L6 | 22M | 20ms | ~400ms | +5% |
| bge-reranker-v2-m3 | 560M | 100ms+ | ~2s | +25% (too slow) |

1. For top-20 reranking, is 300ms acceptable with daemon pre-warming?

description:
## Task: Benchmark bge-small-en-v1.5 (baseline only unless eligible)

### IMPORTANT
Pre-2025-11 baseline unless a post-2025-10 variant exists in embedding_candidates_2025_11+.json.

## Purpose
Strong short-query baseline that demonstrates instruction-tuning benefits.
bge-small is notable for its query instruction prefix which improves retrieval quality.

## Model Details
- Source: BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5
- Parameters: 33.4M
- Dimensions: 384
- Context: 512 tokens
- MTEB Retrieval: ~51 (notably higher than MiniLM for retrieval)
- Special: Uses instruction prefix for queries

## Architecture
```rust
pub struct BgeSmallEmbedder {
    session: ort::Session,
    tokenizer: tokenizers::Tokenizer,
    dimensions: usize,    // 384
    max_length: usize,    // 512
    name: String,
}

impl Embedder for BgeSmallEmbedder {
    fn embed_batch(&self, texts: &[&str]) -> Result<Vec<Vec<f32>>> {
        // BGE uses [CLS] token embedding (not mean pooling!)
        // For queries: prefix with "Represent this sentence for searching relevant passages: "
        // For documents: no prefix needed
        
        let encodings = self.tokenizer.encode_batch(texts.to_vec(), true)?;
        let max_len = encodings.iter().map(|e| e.len()).max().unwrap_or(0).min(self.max_length);
        
        let input_ids = build_padded_tensor(&encodings, max_len, 0);
        let attention_mask = build_attention_mask(&encodings, max_len);
        let token_type_ids = build_zeros_tensor(texts.len(), max_len);
        
        let outputs = self.session.run(ort::inputs![
            "input_ids" => input_ids,
            "attention_mask" => attention_mask,
            "token_type_ids" => token_type_ids,
        ]?)?;
        
        // BGE uses CLS token (position 0) as the embedding
        let hidden = outputs[0].extract_tensor::<f32>()?;
        let mut results = Vec::with_capacity(texts.len());
        for i in 0..texts.len() {
            let mut cls_embedding = (0..self.dimensions)
                .map(|d| hidden[[i, 0, d]])
                .collect::<Vec<f32>>();
            l2_normalize(&mut cls_embedding);
            results.push(cls_embedding);
        }
        Ok(results)
    }
    
    fn dimensions(&self) -> usize { 384 }
    fn model_name(&self) -> &str { &self.name }
    fn supports_mrl(&self) -> bool { false }
}
```

## Key Differences from MiniLM
1. Uses [CLS] pooling instead of mean pooling
2. Instruction prefix for queries improves retrieval by 2-5%
3. Slightly larger (33M vs 22M) but same output dimensions
4. Better training data (BAAI curated for retrieval)

## Benchmark Focus
- Compare CLS-pooling vs mean-pooling quality
- Instruction prefix impact: with vs without prefix
- Speed: how much slower than MiniLM due to extra params?
- Quality: does the 2-5% MTEB improvement translate to our data?
- Short query performance (tweet-length queries)

## Location

results/bge_small_en_v1_5_baseline.json

## Validation and Tests

- L2 normalization of CLS embedding
- Output dimensions always 384
- Max length truncation at 512
- Empty input handling
- Token type IDs all zeros

### Integration tests

- Compare query with/without instruction prefix:
  - Prefixed queries should have higher recall in retrieval
- Known relevant pairs have higher cosine similarity
- Batch consistency: batch embedding matches individual

description:
## Overview
Design and implement a **warm model daemon** that keeps embedding + reranker models resident for instant CPU inference. Eliminates cold-start latency for interactive CLI.

## Core Requirements
- UDS IPC with MessagePack
- Protocol versioning for forward compatibility
- Lazy-load models; keep warm with idle timeout
- Nice/ionice + bounded thread pool (rayon)
- Graceful fallback if daemon is unavailable

## Protocol (MessagePack)
Include a version field in every request/response:
```rust
struct Envelope<T> { version: u8, payload: T }
```

```rust
enum DaemonRequest {
  Embed { texts: Vec<String>, model: String },
  Rerank { query: String, documents: Vec<String>, model: String },
  Health,
  Shutdown,
  Stats,
}

enum DaemonResponse {
  Embeddings { vectors: Vec<Vec<f32>> },
  Reranked { scores: Vec<f32> },
  Health { uptime_secs: u64, requests_served: u64 },
  Error { message: String },
}
```

## Being Nice to the System
- `nice(10)` CPU priority
- `ionice -c3` idle I/O
- `setrlimit` memory + open files
- Rayon threads: `min(4, num_cpus/2)`
- Idle timeout unload + exit

## Phases
1. Daemon core (UDS, protocol)
2. Multi-model lazy loading
3. Resource management + monitoring
4. Client integration + fallback

## Validation & Tests
### Unit tests
- Protocol serialize/deserialize compatibility
- Version negotiation behavior
- Idle timeout triggers unload

### Integration tests

description:
## Task: Benchmark EmbeddingGemma-300M

Evaluate Google DeepMind EmbeddingGemma-300M, the SOTA sub-500M parameter embedding model.

## Model Details
- Source: Google DeepMind (released October 2025)
- Parameters: 308M
- Architecture: Modified Gemma with embedding-optimized training
- Dimensions: 768 (supports MRL truncation to 256/384/512)
- Context: 2048 tokens
- MTEB: Reported 55+ on retrieval (state-of-the-art for size class)
- Speed: Sub-15ms on EdgeTPU; estimated 30-80ms on modern CPU

## Why This Model Is Critical
EmbeddingGemma represents Google best effort at a tiny-but-powerful embedding model:
1. MRL support: Truncate to 256 dims with minimal quality loss
2. Instruction-tuned: Different prefixes for queries vs documents
3. Strong on short text: Optimized for mobile/edge = good for tweets
4. ONNX exportable: Should work with ort crate

## Architecture
```rust
pub struct EmbeddingGemmaEmbedder {
    session: ort::Session,
    tokenizer: tokenizers::Tokenizer,
    native_dims: usize,          // 768
    target_dims: Option<usize>,  // MRL truncation target
    max_length: usize,           // 2048 tokens
    mode: GemmaMode,             // Query vs Document
    name: String,
}

enum GemmaMode {
    Query,     // Prefixes with "Represent this query for retrieval: "
    Document,  // Prefixes with "Represent this document for retrieval: "
}

impl Embedder for EmbeddingGemmaEmbedder {
    fn embed_batch(&self, texts: &[&str]) -> Result<Vec<Vec<f32>>> {
        // 1. Apply instruction prefix based on mode
        let prefixed: Vec<String> = texts.iter().map(|t| {
            match self.mode {
                GemmaMode::Query => format!("Represent this query for retrieval: {}", t),
                GemmaMode::Document => format!("Represent this document for retrieval: {}", t),
            }
        }).collect();
        
        // 2. Tokenize with padding
        let encodings = self.tokenizer.encode_batch(
            prefixed.iter().map(|s| s.as_str()).collect::<Vec<_>>(),
            true
        )?;
        
        // 3. Run ONNX inference (transformer forward pass)
        let max_len = encodings.iter().map(|e| e.len()).max().unwrap_or(0)
            .min(self.max_length);
        let input_ids = build_padded_tensor(&encodings, max_len, 0);
        let attention_mask = build_attention_mask(&encodings, max_len);
        
        let outputs = self.session.run(ort::inputs![
            "input_ids" => input_ids,
            "attention_mask" => attention_mask,
        ]?)?;
        
        // 4. Pool: mean of last hidden state (respecting attention mask)
        let hidden = outputs[0].extract_tensor::<f32>()?;
        let mut results = Vec::with_capacity(texts.len());
        for i in 0..texts.len() {
            let mut pooled = mean_pool_with_mask(&hidden, i, max_len, self.native_dims, &attention_mask);
            
            // 5. MRL truncation if specified
            if let Some(target) = self.target_dims {
                pooled.truncate(target);
            }
            l2_normalize(&mut pooled);
            results.push(pooled);
        }
        Ok(results)
    }
    
    fn dimensions(&self) -> usize { self.target_dims.unwrap_or(self.native_dims) }
    fn model_name(&self) -> &str { &self.name }
    fn supports_mrl(&self) -> bool { true }
}
```

## Benchmark Focus

### Speed Profiling
- Cold start (model load from disk, ONNX session creation)
- First inference vs steady state
- Batch efficiency curves: batch 1, 4, 8, 16, 32
- Memory footprint (FP32 vs quantized)
- Thread scaling (1, 2, 4 threads via ORT intra_op_num_threads)

### Quality Profiling
- Full 768-dim quality (ceiling)
- MRL truncation: 256, 384, 512 dims
- Short text (tweets < 280 chars)
- Medium text (DMs, ~1000 chars)
- Long text (Grok conversations, 2000+ chars)
- Cross-type query-to-doc retrieval

### Feasibility Assessment
1. Is 308M too large for instant CLI response on CPU?
2. Does INT8 quantization (via ONNX quantize_dynamic) help enough?
3. Is MRL-256 competitive with static models at their native dims?
4. Does instruction-tuning matter for our mixed-content queries?
5. How much does daemon pre-warming help (cold 2s vs warm 50ms)?

## ONNX Export (if not available pre-exported)
```bash
pip install optimum[onnxruntime]
```

title: Task: Implement daemon client with auto-spawn and fallback
description:
## Task: Implement Daemon Client with Auto-Spawn and Fallback

Build the client library that xf uses to communicate with the model daemon.
The client is the primary interface between xf search commands and the warm model daemon.

## Architecture

### Socket Discovery
- Default path: /tmp/xf-daemon-{uid}.sock (or XF_DAEMON_SOCK env override)
- Lock file: /tmp/xf-daemon-{uid}.lock (prevents double-spawn)
- PID file: /tmp/xf-daemon-{uid}.pid (for status/stop commands)

### Auto-Spawn Protocol
```rust
pub struct DaemonClient {
    socket_path: PathBuf,
    connect_timeout: Duration,   // 2s default
    request_timeout: Duration,   // 30s default
    max_retries: u8,             // 3 default
}

impl DaemonClient {
    /// Connect to existing daemon or spawn a new one
    pub async fn connect_or_spawn(config: &DaemonConfig) -> Result<Self> {
        // 1. Try connect to existing socket
        // 2. If ENOENT/ECONNREFUSED: acquire lock file
        // 3. Spawn daemon as background process (fork+exec)
        // 4. Wait for socket to appear (poll with backoff)
        // 5. Connect and send Health check
        // 6. Release lock file
    }
}
```

### Spawn Sequence
1. Check lock file (flock, non-blocking)
2. If locked: another client is spawning, wait for socket
3. Fork daemon process with: nice(10), ionice(idle), setsid()
4. Daemon writes PID file after socket bind succeeds
5. Client polls for socket existence (50ms intervals, max 5s)
6. Client connects and verifies Health response

### Connection Retry Policy
- Exponential backoff: 50ms, 100ms, 200ms (3 retries)
- On all retries exhausted: fall back to direct inference
- Socket EOF during request: single reconnect attempt
- Daemon crash (EPIPE): log warning, fallback immediately

### Fallback to Direct Inference
```rust
pub enum InferenceMode {
    Daemon(DaemonClient),
    Direct(Box<dyn Embedder>), // Falls back to loading model in-process
}

impl InferenceMode {
    /// Transparently handles daemon failure
    pub async fn embed(&self, texts: &[&str]) -> Result<Vec<Vec<f32>>> {
        match self {
            Self::Daemon(client) => {
                match client.send_embed(texts).await {
                    Ok(result) => Ok(result),
                    Err(e) => {
                        tracing::warn!("Daemon failed ({e}), falling back to direct");
                        // Load model in-process, cache for subsequent calls
                        self.upgrade_to_direct().await
                    }
                }
            }
            Self::Direct(embedder) => embedder.embed_batch(texts),
        }
    }
}
```

### MessagePack Protocol (matches bd-1oy)
```rust
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct Request {
    version: u8,      // Protocol version (1)
    id: u64,          // Request ID for correlation
    payload: RequestPayload,
}

enum RequestPayload {
    Health,
    Embed { texts: Vec<String>, model: String, dims: Option<usize> },
    Rerank { query: String, documents: Vec<String>, model: String },
    Shutdown,
    Status, // Returns loaded models, memory usage, uptime
}
```

## Location
src/daemon/client.rs
src/daemon/spawn.rs

## Validation and Tests
### Unit tests
- Socket path construction (with/without env override)
- Retry backoff timing sequence
- Lock file acquire/release semantics
- Request serialization round-trip
- Fallback mode transition logic
- PID file parsing and validation

### Integration tests
- Spawn daemon, send Health, Embed, Status, Shutdown
- Simulate daemon crash mid-request, verify fallback activates
- Simulate daemon not responding (timeout), verify retry then fallback
- Concurrent clients: two clients connect simultaneously
- Lock file prevents double-spawn race condition

### E2E script (detailed logging)
- scripts/daemon/client_e2e.sh
  - Logs: socket path, spawn timing, connection attempts
  - Logs: request latencies (connect + roundtrip separately)
  - Tests: cold connect (no daemon running) measures spawn time
  - Tests: warm connect (daemon already up) measures connect time
  - Tests: fallback path (kill daemon mid-request, verify recovery)
  - Tests: concurrent requests from multiple processes
  - Cleanup: sends Shutdown, verifies socket + PID file removed

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Auto-spawn works reliably with lock file protection
- [ ] Fallback to direct inference is transparent to callers
- [ ] No user-visible errors when daemon is down
- [ ] Retry policy with exponential backoff implemented
- [ ] Lock file prevents double-spawn races
- [ ] PID file enables daemon management (stop/status)
- [ ] Logs capture: connection attempts, fallback events, spawn timing
- [ ] E2E script passes all scenarios with detailed logging
notes:
### Optimization review
- Handle **daemon overload** response explicitly: treat as retryable once, then fall back to direct inference to preserve responsiveness.
- Add **jitter** to backoff to avoid thundering herd when multiple clients spawn.

1. **Resolve archive path**
   - Precedence: `--archive` > config default (if stored) > none.
   - If none, **skip archive checks** and emit a warning + suggestion (do not fail).
2. **Run checks**
   - Archive checks: `check_required_files`, `check_json_structure`, `check_duplicate_ids`, `check_timestamp_consistency`.
   - Database checks: `Storage::database_health_checks()` (integrity, FTS, orphans, table counts).

   - Performance checks: `run_performance_benchmarks`.
3. **Aggregate results**
   - Stable ordering: category order (Archive → Database → Index → Performance), then name.
   - Summary counts: pass/warn/error/critical + total.
4. **Output**
   - Text: section headers, per-check emoji, summary line, then suggestions list.

title: Natural Language Date Filtering
description:
## Overview

Enable human‑friendly date expressions for `--since/--until` with **clear, deterministic semantics**, local‑time interpretation, and UTC comparison.

## Supported Expressions (must be documented + tested)

### Absolute
- ISO dates: `YYYY-MM-DD`, `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ`, `YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM` (local).
- Month/year: `Jan 2023`, `January 2023`, `2024-02` → full month range.
- Quarter: `Q1 2024`, `Q4 2022` → quarter range.
- Seasons: `spring 2023`, `summer 2023`, `fall 2023`, `winter 2023` (winter spans Dec–Feb with year boundary).

### Relative / Named
- `today`, `yesterday`.
- `last|past N days/weeks/months/years`.
- `N days/weeks/months/years ago`.
- `this month`, `last month`, `this year`, `last year`.
- `weekend`, `weekdays` (range covering the most recent weekend/weekday block relative to base time).

## Semantics

- **Ranges:** convert to inclusive start/end instants (start of day 00:00:00 local, end 23:59:59 local), then store/compare in UTC.
- **Point dates:** map to start of day (00:00:00 local) unless `prefer_end` is requested.
- `--since` uses range **start**, `--until` uses range **end**.
- Error messages must include the original input and 2–3 example formats.
- `--verbose` echoes parsed range in UTC and local time for clarity.

## Test Strategy

- **Unit:** deterministic parsing via fixed base time; cover each expression type and boundary conditions (month lengths, leap years, DST transitions).
- **Integration:** CLI parsing for `--since/--until` plus verbose output; ensure ISO fallback still works.
- **E2E:** `tests/e2e/date_parse_test.sh` runs representative expressions, validates output + exit codes, logs command/stdout/stderr/duration.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Natural language expressions accepted for `--since/--until`.
- [ ] ISO inputs remain supported with no regressions.
- [ ] Clear error messages with examples.
- [ ] Deterministic unit tests (no wall‑clock dependency).
- [ ] Integration + E2E tests with detailed logs.

description:
## Overview

This epic tracks the comprehensive UX/UI overhaul to bring xf from functional to premium-quality.
The goal is Stripe-level polish: consistent, intuitive, visually appealing, and delightful to use.

## Background & Motivation

A thorough UX audit revealed numerous opportunities for improvement:

1. **Visual inconsistency**: Divider widths vary (40, 60, 65 chars), emoji usage is sporadic, color usage lacks hierarchy
2. **Poor information design**: Raw scores shown to users (0.75), long numeric IDs displayed, dates in ISO format
3. **Error UX**: Messages are correct but not helpful; missing suggestions and context
4. **Missing polish**: No timing feedback, no version info, no graceful empty states
5. **Accessibility gaps**: No --no-color flag, inconsistent terminal support

## Success Criteria

- Users describe xf as 'polished' and 'professional'
- Error messages include actionable suggestions
- Output is scannable with clear visual hierarchy
- Accessibility: works in all terminal environments
- Consistent design language throughout

## Implementation Approach

This epic is broken into feature beads by domain (visual design, search results, etc.), each with specific implementation tasks. Features can be worked on in parallel.

## Design Principles

1. Consistency over cleverness: Same patterns everywhere
2. Progressive disclosure: Basic info first, details on demand

title: Search Results: Premium Display
description:
## Purpose

Transform search result display from functional to delightful. Search is the core user action and should feel fast, informative, and easy to scan.

## Current Problems

1. **Raw BM25 scores shown**: Output like '(0.75)' is meaningless to users. They don't know if 0.75 is good or bad, or what the scale is.

2. **Long numeric IDs displayed**: Tweet IDs like '1234567890123456789' waste horizontal space and provide no value to users in normal operation.

3. **Result numbers are dimmed**: The '1.' prefix is dimmed, making it hard to scan and reference results.

4. **No visual separation**: Results blur together without clear boundaries. Difficult to scan quickly.

5. **Dates are ISO format**: '2024-01-15 10:30' is less friendly than 'Jan 15' or '3 days ago'.

6. **Empty results message is plain**: 'No results found.' could suggest query modifications.

7. **No timing shown**: Users don't see how fast searches are, missing a key selling point.

## Solution

### Score Display
Replace raw scores with human-friendly indicators:
- 0.8+ = 'High relevance' or ★★★★★
- 0.5-0.8 = 'Medium relevance' or ★★★☆☆
- <0.5 = 'Low relevance' or ★★☆☆☆
Or hide scores entirely (most search engines don't show them).

### ID Display
- Hide IDs by default in text output
- Show truncated form on demand: '1234...6789'
- Always include full ID in JSON output

### Visual Cards
Add clear separation between results:
```
┌─ 1 ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
│ TWEET                                           Jan 15, 2024
│ Tweet text with **highlighted** matches...
│ ♥ 42  ↺ 12
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```

### Dates
Use relative format with smart thresholds:
- < 24h: '3 hours ago'
- < 7d: '3 days ago'
- < 1y: 'Jan 15'
- >= 1y: 'Jan 15, 2023'

### Empty Results
Provide helpful suggestions:
'No results for "xyzzy". Try:
  • Using different keywords
  • Checking spelling
  • Removing filters'

### Timing
Add to output: 'Found 42 results in 3ms'

## Files to Modify

- src/main.rs: print_result(), cmd_search()
- src/repl.rs: print_results(), run_search()
- src/model.rs: Possibly add helper methods

## Dependencies

Depends on Visual Design System for consistent styling.

## Purpose

### Error Format Standard

```
✗ [Brief error title]

     • First option
     • Second option

```

## Epic: Search & Indexing Performance Optimization

### Executive Summary
This epic drives a comprehensive performance + correctness overhaul of xf’s search and indexing. The goal is **p50 hybrid/semantic <50ms** on the standard corpus, **indexing 50K docs <120s**, and **identical outputs** (isomorphic ordering/content) for the same inputs. All changes must remain privacy-first (no network paths) and deterministic.

### Updated Bottlenecks (Root Causes)
1. **Embedding reload per search (CRITICAL)** — every hybrid/semantic search reloads embeddings from SQLite and rebuilds the vector index (dominates latency).
2. **N+1 document lookups (CRITICAL)** — semantic/hybrid fetches doc bodies one-by-one instead of a single batch Tantivy query.
3. **Sequential embedding generation (CRITICAL)** — CPU-bound embedding generation runs on a single core and wastes available parallelism.
4. **Stats N+1 queries (MEDIUM)** — `xf stats` issues 10+ COUNT(*) queries instead of one consolidated query.
5. **Embedding identity collisions (CORRECTNESS)** — `embeddings` table uses doc_id-only PK, causing tweet/like collisions and incorrect semantic results.
6. **RRF clones (LOW/CPU)** — avoidable clones in fusion path increase allocations (low but easy win).

title: Feature: Implement embedding caching to eliminate per-search reload
description:
## Problem Statement
Every hybrid or semantic search triggers a full reload of all embeddings from SQLite:

```rust
// src/main.rs:929-949 (current implementation)
let embeddings = storage.load_all_embeddings()?;  // FULL TABLE SCAN every search\!
let mut index = VectorIndex::new(384);
for (doc_id, doc_type, embedding) in embeddings {
    index.add(doc_id, doc_type, embedding);
}
```

### Impact
- **Latency**: Adds 500-2000ms to every search (depending on archive size)
- **Memory**: Creates new allocations for each search, causing GC pressure
- **I/O**: Unnecessary disk reads for unchanged data
- **User Experience**: Unacceptable for interactive use

### Root Cause
The VectorIndex is created as a local variable in cmd_search(), so it's rebuilt from scratch on every invocation. There's no caching or persistence of the loaded embeddings.

## Solution: OnceLock Singleton Pattern

Use Rust's `std::sync::OnceLock` to create a lazily-initialized, thread-safe singleton:

```rust
use std::sync::OnceLock;

static VECTOR_INDEX: OnceLock<VectorIndex> = OnceLock::new();

fn get_or_init_vector_index(storage: &Storage) -> Result<&'static VectorIndex> {
    VECTOR_INDEX.get_or_try_init(|| {
        let embeddings = storage.load_all_embeddings()?;
        let mut index = VectorIndex::new(384);
        for (doc_id, doc_type, embedding) in embeddings {
            index.add(doc_id, doc_type, embedding);
        }
        Ok(index)
    })
}
```

### Why OnceLock?
- **Thread-safe**: Safe for concurrent access (future REPL parallelism)
- **Lazy**: Only loads when first needed
- **Zero-cost after init**: Subsequent accesses are just pointer reads
- **No external dependencies**: Part of std library

## Cache Invalidation Strategy
The cache must be invalidated when:
1. User runs `xf index` (new embeddings generated)
2. Database file is modified externally

Detection approach (see xf-48):
- Store database mtime or version number at cache creation
- Check before each search if stale
- If stale, reload (rare operation)

## Expected Performance Impact
| Metric | Before | After | Improvement |
|--------|--------|-------|-------------|
| First search | 1500ms | 1500ms | 0% (cold start) |
| Subsequent searches | 1500ms | 30ms | 98% reduction |
| Memory per search | +73MB | 0 | No new allocations |

## Child Tasks
- xf-40: Add OnceLock static for VectorIndex
- xf-41: Modify cmd_search to use cached VectorIndex
- xf-48: Add cache invalidation detection
- xf-49: Unit tests for caching behavior

title: Feature: Consolidate stats N+1 queries into single query
description:
## Problem Statement
The `xf stats` command runs 10+ individual COUNT(*) queries:

```rust
// src/main.rs cmd_stats (current implementation)
let tweets = storage.get_tweet_count()?;       // Query 1
let likes = storage.get_like_count()?;         // Query 2
let dms = storage.get_dm_count()?;             // Query 3
let grok = storage.get_grok_count()?;          // Query 4
let followers = storage.get_follower_count()?; // Query 5
let following = storage.get_following_count()?;// Query 6
let blocks = storage.get_block_count()?;       // Query 7
let mutes = storage.get_mute_count()?;         // Query 8
let first_date = storage.get_first_tweet_date()?; // Query 9
let last_date = storage.get_last_tweet_date()?;   // Query 10
// ... more queries for --detailed
```

### Impact
- **Latency**: 10+ round trips to SQLite (~5-10ms each)
- **Total time**: 50-100ms for basic stats
- **Overhead**: Each query has connection/prepare/execute overhead

### Root Cause
Each getter method was written independently for single-purpose use. No batch method exists.

## Solution: Consolidated Query

Create a single method that returns all counts:

```rust
pub struct AllCounts {
    pub tweets: i64,
    pub likes: i64,
    pub dms: i64,
    pub grok_messages: i64,
    pub followers: i64,
    pub following: i64,
    pub blocks: i64,
    pub mutes: i64,
    pub conversations: i64,
    pub first_tweet_date: Option<DateTime<Utc>>,
    pub last_tweet_date: Option<DateTime<Utc>>,
}

impl Storage {
    pub fn get_all_counts(&self) -> Result<AllCounts> {
        // Single query using subqueries or UNION ALL
        let sql = "
            SELECT
                (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM tweets) as tweets,
                (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM likes) as likes,
                (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM direct_messages) as dms,
                (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM grok_messages) as grok,
                (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM followers) as followers,
                (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM following) as following,
                (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM blocks) as blocks,
                (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM mutes) as mutes,
                (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT conversation_id) FROM direct_messages) as conversations,
                (SELECT MIN(created_at) FROM tweets) as first_tweet,
                (SELECT MAX(created_at) FROM tweets) as last_tweet
        ";
        
        let row = self.conn.query_row(sql, [], |row| { ... })?;
        Ok(AllCounts { ... })
    }
}
```

### Why Subqueries?
- Single round trip to SQLite
- SQLite optimizes subquery execution
- All counts computed in one pass through each table
- Atomic snapshot of data (no race conditions between counts)

## Expected Performance Impact
| Metric | Before | After | Improvement |
|--------|--------|-------|-------------|
| Stats latency | 50-100ms | 5-10ms | 90% reduction |
| DB round trips | 10+ | 1 | 90% reduction |

## Backward Compatibility
- Keep individual get_*_count() methods for other callers
- AllCounts struct is additive, not breaking

title: Feature: Eliminate unnecessary clones in RRF fusion
description:
## Problem Statement
The RRF fusion algorithm clones SearchResult objects unnecessarily:

```rust
// src/hybrid.rs:129-134 (current implementation)
for (rank, hit) in lexical.iter().enumerate() {
    entry.rrf += 1.0 / (RRF_K + rank as f32 + 1.0);
    entry.lexical_rank = Some(rank);
    lexical_results.insert(hit.id.clone(), hit.clone());  // CLONE\!
    doc_types.insert(hit.id.clone(), hit.result_type.to_string());  // CLONE\!
}
```

And later:
```rust
// src/hybrid.rs:153-154
doc_type: doc_types.get(&doc_id).cloned().unwrap_or_default(),  // CLONE\!
lexical: lexical_results.remove(&doc_id),  // Move, but cloned earlier
```

### Impact
- **Allocations**: ~400 heap allocations per search (100 results × 4 clones)
- **Memory**: Temporary duplication of result data
- **GC pressure**: More allocations = more deallocation work

### Root Cause
The code was written for simplicity, storing cloned data in HashMaps. The FusedHit struct owns its data rather than borrowing.

## Solution: Lifetime-Based Borrowing

Refactor to use references and indices instead of clones:

```rust
pub struct FusedHit<'a> {
    pub doc_id: &'a str,  // Borrow from input
    pub doc_type: &'a str,
    pub score: f32,
    pub lexical: Option<&'a SearchResult>,  // Reference, not owned
    pub in_both: bool,
}

pub fn rrf_fuse<'a>(
    lexical: &'a [SearchResult],
    semantic: &[VectorSearchResult],
    limit: usize,
    offset: usize,
) -> Vec<FusedHit<'a>> {
    // Store indices instead of clones
    let mut lexical_indices: HashMap<&str, usize> = HashMap::new();
    
    for (rank, hit) in lexical.iter().enumerate() {
        lexical_indices.insert(&hit.id, rank);  // &str key, usize value
    }
    
    // Build results using references
    FusedHit {
        doc_id: &hit.id,
        lexical: Some(&lexical[idx]),  // Reference into input slice
        // ...
    }
}
```

### Why Lifetimes?
- Zero-copy: No heap allocations for result data
- Compile-time safety: Rust guarantees references are valid
- Same API ergonomics: Callers don't notice the change

## Complexity Considerations
This is a **medium-complexity refactor**:
- Requires adding lifetime parameters to FusedHit
- Callers must ensure lexical slice outlives FusedHit usage
- May propagate lifetime requirements upstream

## Expected Performance Impact
| Metric | Before | After | Improvement |
|--------|--------|-------|-------------|
| Allocations/search | ~400 | ~50 | 87% reduction |
| RRF fusion time | ~2ms | ~0.5ms | 75% reduction |

title: Bug: Embedding identity collisions (doc_id-only PK)
description:
## Problem
The `embeddings` table uses `doc_id` as the sole primary key. Tweets and likes frequently share the same `doc_id` (tweet ID), which means embeddings for one type overwrite the other. This is a correctness bug: semantic/hybrid search may return the wrong text or incorrect similarity for the requested type.

### Evidence
- Tweets and likes share IDs by design (like references the original tweet ID).
- Current schema: `PRIMARY KEY (doc_id)` in `embeddings`.
- Retrieval APIs (`get_embedding`, `get_embedding_hash`, `get_embedding_by_hash`, `load_all_embeddings`) do not accept/return type-qualified identities.

### Impact
- Incorrect embeddings used for semantic/hybrid results.
- Content-hash de-duplication can reuse embeddings across types incorrectly.
- Potentially wrong ranking and mismatched metadata at retrieval time.

## Goal
Ensure embeddings are keyed by `(doc_id, doc_type)` so that semantic search results are correct and deterministic for mixed-type archives.

## Proposed Fix (High-Level)
1. Bump schema version and rebuild `embeddings` table with a composite primary key.
2. Update all embedding APIs to include `doc_type` in lookups and inserts.
3. Update generation code to pass `doc_type` everywhere.
4. Add regression tests that create collisions (tweet + like same ID) and verify correct embeddings and results.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Embeddings table primary key is `(doc_id, doc_type)`.
- All embedding APIs are type-aware; no ambiguous lookups remain.
- Regression test proves tweet/like with same ID return correct embeddings.
- `xf index` still rebuilds cleanly; semantic/hybrid outputs remain isomorphic within type.

## Notes
- Embeddings are derived data; dropping/rebuilding is acceptable with a schema version bump.
- Coordinate with the persistent vector index work to ensure doc_type is stored and used consistently.

title: Build architecture map + core workflow understanding
description:
Goal:
- Produce a high-level architecture map of xf: major modules, data flow, and runtime workflows.

Context:
- Requires prior understanding of AGENTS.md/README constraints.

Steps:
1) Inventory key modules in /data/projects/xf/src (main.rs, parser.rs, search.rs, storage.rs, index.rs, etc.).
2) Trace core flows: indexing path (input archive -> parse -> storage/index), search path (query parse -> execution -> result formatting).
3) Note data boundaries: DB (SQLite), search index (Tantivy), file I/O paths, and serialization formats.
4) Record a module graph (imports, public APIs, and cross-module calls).

Acceptance:
- A concise but complete architecture summary that identifies the main pipeline stages, storage layers, and execution entry points.
- List of files/functions that are hot paths or correctness-critical.
notes:
Architecture map (high level):
- Entry point: src/main.rs wires CLI (Cli/Commands) to command handlers: index/search/stats/tweet/list/export/config/update/completions.
- CLI definitions: src/cli.rs declares subcommands + many flags (types/limit/offset/sort/since/until/replies/context/fields, etc.). Some flags are not yet wired in main.rs (noted for later correctness checks).
- Core modules (src/lib.rs): parser, model, storage (SQLite), search (Tantivy), config/logging/perf/error.

Indexing flow:
1) xf index <archive> (main.rs cmd_index): validate archive/data/, resolve db/index paths, optionally clear existing data.
2) ArchiveParser (parser.rs) parses JS-wrapped JSON (window.YTD.*) with rayon; parse_manifest -> ArchiveInfo; parse_tweets/likes/dms/grok/followers/etc into model types.
3) Storage::open (storage.rs) opens SQLite, sets pragmas, migrates schema, and stores data into normalized tables + FTS5 virtual tables.
4) SearchEngine::open (search.rs) opens/creates Tantivy index; writer adds documents for each data type (id/text/text_prefix/type/created_at/metadata) and commits.

Search flow:
1) xf search <query> (main.rs cmd_search): open SearchEngine and Storage; map DataType -> search::DocType; call SearchEngine::search with limit+offset.
2) SearchEngine::search (search.rs) uses Tantivy QueryParser (text + prefix field) and optional type filter; collects TopDocs; builds SearchResult with highlights (snippet generator) and metadata (stored JSON).
3) main.rs formats results to json/json pretty/csv/compact/text (with highlight -> ANSI conversion in print_result).

Data boundaries:
- Input: archive files under <archive>/data/*.js with JS prefix; parser tolerates whitespace and trailing semicolons.
- Storage: SQLite schema for tweets/likes/dms/grok + FTS5 tables; metadata in archive_info/meta tables.
- Search index: Tantivy index under XF_INDEX; schema fields include id, text, text_prefix (prefix matching), type, created_at, metadata.

Hot paths / correctness-critical:
- parser.rs: parse_js_file, parse_* per datatype; date parsing; numeric parsing; message aggregation.
- search.rs: schema construction, index_* methods, query parsing, snippet generation.
- storage.rs: schema/migrations + store_* insertions and FTS5 updates.

- src/main.rs: command dispatcher; cmd_index -> ArchiveParser::parse_* -> Storage::store_* + SearchEngine::index_* -> writer.commit + reload. cmd_search -> SearchEngine::search -> output formatting; cmd_stats/tweet/list/export/config/update are stubs/partial (yellow warnings) in main.

- benches/search_perf.rs: synthetic benchmarks invoke SearchEngine and Storage directly; provides baseline for search/index/storage; uses TempDir and synthetic models.

Multi-hop flow traces:
1) xf index -> main.rs cmd_index -> ArchiveParser::parse_tweets -> model::Tweet -> Storage::store_tweets (SQLite inserts + FTS5) -> SearchEngine::index_tweets (Tantivy doc) -> commit + reload.
2) xf search -> main.rs cmd_search -> SearchEngine::search -> QueryParser + TopDocs -> SnippetGenerator -> model::SearchResult -> main.rs output formatter (json/csv/text/compact).
